Analysis shows that we will need to borrow a minimum £82.4 million to maintain liquidity based on current forecasts.

findings.paper_title: For Cabinet - 1. Financial Monitoring Q3 (Informal Cabinet - Clean) - Copy
findings.headline: Savings programme underperforming: £700k (2.6%) of savings targets at risk of not landing
findings.detail: The £26.4m savings target is forecast to deliver only £25.7m (97.35%). Of the gap, £192k is at amber risk and £508k at significant (red) risk. Specific shortfalls include: £158k Community Safety vacancies (red), £187k Home to School Transport (amber), £250k corporate estate reshaping (won't be achieved due to ICB changes), and £100k education deferred pensions (red). The shortfalls are being offset by underspends elsewhere, but this is masking a pattern of savings not delivering as planned.
findings.matters: Savings shortfalls are early warning of budget control issues. When £700k of identified efficiency cuts fail to land, it signals either planning weakness or that service pressures are outrunning mitigation capacity.
findings.figures: Total target £26.434m. Forecast delivery £25.734m. At amber £192k (0.73%). At red £508k (1.92%). Community Safety vacancy target miss £158k. Corporate estate reshaping £250k (full shortfall).
findings.quote: Currently, £192k (0.73%) is at amber risk of not being achieved this financial year, and schemes totalling £508k (1.92%) are at significant risk of not being achieved. The schemes at most risk of not being delivered this year are: £158k of the Community Safety Vacancy Management target (target £220k) showing as high risk (Red rated). £250k of benefit realisation from reshaping of corporate estate. This will not be achieved due to changes with the ICB.

findings.paper_title: For Cabinet - 1. Financial Monitoring Q3 (Informal Cabinet - Clean) - Copy
findings.headline: Adult Social Care £2.5m overspend driven by placement costs and mental health demand, with £3m growth bid needed for 2026/27
findings.detail: ASC is overspending by £2.5m at Q3. The core issue is external care placement costs (£3.5m) and mental health services (£1.3m) both driven by demand and fee inflation. The council has submitted a £3m growth bid for 2026/27 in MTFS proposals, signalling this is structural, not one-off. The £100k improvement from Q2 came from ICB funding help, not resolved underlying pressure.
findings.matters: ASC is typically the largest and least-controllable spend line in local government. An overspend that requires a growth bid signals the council cannot absorb demand-led pressures from base budget, raising questions about sustainability of future positions.
findings.figures: £2.510m overspend (0.4% of service budget). Third-party placements £3.461m adverse. Mental Health £1.297m adverse. Growth bid £3.0m for 2026/27.
findings.quote: Adult Social Care is reporting an overspend of £2.510 million. The current overspend relates to cost pressures within External Care Budgets (including the Transforming Care Programme): £3.461 million in respect third party / placement costs, both demand and average fees. Mental Health overspend of £1.297 million relating to demand and complexity. The MTFS proposals include a growth bid of £3 million for 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: For Cabinet - 1. Financial Monitoring Q3 (Informal Cabinet - Clean) - Copy
findings.headline: DSG deficit forecast to reach £124 million by March 2026 with government solution still unclear
findings.detail: The cumulative Dedicated Schools Grant deficit is forecast to grow from £78.5m to £124.1m after an in-year loss of £45.5m (up £533k from Q2). This reflects surging demand for Education, Health and Care Plans and specialist provision outside mainstream schools. The government's Statutory Override protecting ring-fenced deficits expires March 2028, but ministers have not explained how the accumulated £124m will be addressed after announcing in November 2025 that SEND costs would transfer to government budgets from 2028/29.
findings.matters: This is the largest financial exposure on the council's balance sheet. Lenders and the finance director must know whether government will absorb legacy deficits or leave them with the council after 2028.
findings.figures: Cumulative deficit £78.537m (1 April 2025), in-year deficit £45.550m, forecast balance £124.087m (31 March 2026). Override expires March 2028.
findings.quote: The cumulative DSG deficit is therefore forecast to reach £124.087 million as at 31 March 2026. The Override expires in March 2028, but the impact on the Council's balances is significant. Government announced as part of its Budget proposals on 26 November 2025 that it intends to absorb SEND costs from Government budgets from 2028/29. However, it is unclear at this stage how Government intends to address the current in-year deficits and historic deficits accumulated up to 31 March 2028.

findings.paper_title: Draft 202627 Budget January Cabinet Report
findings.headline: Adults and children's services facing £12.1 million in annual cost pressures from wage and NI inflation
findings.detail: The council is funding inflationary uplifts to care providers of £7.908 million for adult services and £4.210 million for children's services to cover national living wage and employers' national insurance contribution changes. Delegation of negotiation authority to directors signals costs may exceed these budgeted amounts.
findings.matters: Significant committed annual cost increases in social care indicate structural service cost inflation that repeats every year and constrains budget flexibility.
findings.figures: £7.908 million for adult service provider uplifts; £4.210 million for children service provider uplifts; total £12.118 million
findings.quote: Approves, subject to approval of the budget by County Council, necessary inflationary uplifts in adults and children services, at a cost of no more than £12.118 million (made up of £7.908 million for adult providers and £4.210 million for children providers).

findings.paper_title: Draft 202627 Budget January Cabinet Report
findings.headline: Council drawing down £1.4 million from reserves to balance 2026/27 budget
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget achieves balance only by drawing £1.4 million net from reserves, with a further £4.2 million drawn in 2027/28 for one-off expenditure. This represents a structural operating deficit being met from accumulated reserves rather than from recurring income.
findings.matters: Using reserves to balance operating budgets signals that recurring revenue does not cover recurring costs, an unsustainable medium-term position.
findings.figures: £1.4 million reserve drawdown for 2026/27; £4.2 million reserve drawdown for 2027/28
findings.quote: The reserve projections include the proposed net drawing of £1.4 million to balance the 2026/27 budget, plus a further £4.2 million for one-off expenditure in 2027/28.

findings.paper_title: Draft 202627 Budget January Cabinet Report
findings.headline: Provisional settlement caused £9.5 million adverse impact, forcing emergency budget revision
findings.detail: The Provisional Local Government Finance Settlement released 17 December 2025 significantly deteriorated funding projections relative to the pre-consultation draft. Grants rolled into core spending power and new burdens created £9.8 million in adverse impacts, with a total emerging budget gap of £9.5 million. The council has lodged concerns about the settlement with Government.
findings.matters: A major mid-cycle funding shock not anticipated at budget publication indicates uncertain external funding and forces reactive budget cuts rather than planned transition.
findings.figures: £9.5 million total adverse impact / emerging budget gap; £9.8 million from grants rolled into CSP and ring-fenced funding
findings.quote: The provisional settlement has unfortunately resulted in a significant deterioration in resources relative to the projections included in the consultation. Total adverse impact of PLGFS / Emerging Budget Gap (9.5)

findings.paper_title: Draft 202627 Budget January Cabinet Report
findings.headline: DSG high needs block deficit projected to exceed £241.6 million by March 2028 when Statutory Override expires
findings.detail: The council's dedicated schools grant high needs block is in deficit, with a forecast balance of £124.1 million at 31 March 2026, and projected to grow to beyond £241.6 million by 31 March 2028 when the Statutory Override mechanism expires. This is a ring-fenced deficit the council is required to carry but will face an accounting cliff in two years.
findings.matters: A massive accumulated deficit in a designated reserve approaching expiry represents a critical financial cliff; lenders need assurance on how the council will address this from 2028 onwards.
findings.figures: £124.1 million deficit at 31 March 2026; £54.4 million deficit budget in 2026/27; cumulative deficit projected to grow to beyond £241.6 million by 31 March 2028
findings.quote: The forecast deficit balance as at 31 March 2026 is £124.1 million. Based on current information it is anticipated that a deficit budget of £54.4 million will be set in 2026/27. The cumulative deficit is projected to grow to beyond £241.6 million by the expected end of Statutory Override on 31 March 2028.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Draft Budget and MTFS
findings.headline: Significant uncertainty remains about true costs of rolled-in grants, with risk that further adverse impacts may emerge as new grant conditions are clarified.
findings.detail: The council is projecting its budget based on incomplete information about its grant allocations. The document explicitly warns: 'Given the significant impact of changes to grants for 2026/27 announced as part of the Provisional Local Government Finance Settlement, there remains a risk that further impacts may arise in future years, and/or through confirmation of the specific terms and conditions of new grants.' The document also states 'The full implications of the changes to the grant framework and the new consolidated grants on the Budget is still being reviewed.'
findings.matters: Downside risk exists where grant conditions and new responsibilities become clearer after budget setting. Unquantified additional pressures may emerge, adding to already unresolved gaps in years 3-4.
findings.figures: 16 grants consolidated into 4 new consolidated grants; 17 funding streams consolidated into Revenue Support Grant; impact 'still being reviewed'
findings.quote: Given the significant impact of changes to grants for 2026/27 announced as part of the Provisional Local Government Finance Settlement, there remains a risk that further impacts may arise in future years, and/or through confirmation of the specific terms and conditions of new grants.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Draft Budget and MTFS
findings.headline: Council is using £1.4 million of non-earmarked reserves in 2026/27 and £4.2 million in 2027/28 to balance budgets.
findings.detail: Rather than achieving budget balance through service changes or savings alone, the council is drawing down reserves to cover recurring cost gaps: 'The 2026/27 budget proposals are balanced with a net transfer from reserves of £1.4 million. The 2027/28 budget proposals are also balanced following the use of £4.2 million use of non-earmarked reserves to fund one-off pressures.' This £5.6 million depletion in two years occurs while unresolved gaps remain in years 3-4.
findings.matters: Using reserves to balance recurring budget gaps is unsustainable and indicates the base budget does not cover ongoing costs. Reserve depletion when future gaps remain unresolved is a warning sign of structural deficit.
findings.figures: £1.4 million reserve use 2026/27; £4.2 million reserve use 2027/28; cumulative £5.6 million in two years
findings.quote: The 2026/27 budget proposals are balanced with a net transfer from reserves of £1.4 million. The 2027/28 budget proposals are also balanced following the use of £4.2 million use of non-earmarked reserves to fund one-off pressures.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Draft Budget and MTFS
findings.headline: Council tax funding is increasing structurally to 72% of base budget by 2028/29, up from 65% in 2026/27, as government grants decline.
findings.detail: The document notes a structural shift in funding sources: 'An ever-increasing amount of GCC's funding comes from Council Tax. With the changes to the funding system this is even more apparent with 65% of GCC's base budget being funded from Council Tax in 2026/27, increasing to 72% by 2028/29.' This reflects government policy that 'higher taxbase authorities can afford to fund more of their spend from internal resources.'
findings.matters: A council funding 72% of its base budget from council tax is exposed to collection risks, taxpayer resistance, and local economic conditions. This structural shift narrows financial flexibility and increases vulnerability to external shocks.
findings.figures: 65% from Council Tax in 2026/27; 72% by 2028/29; government grants declining from 35% to 28% of funding base
findings.quote: An ever-increasing amount of GCC's funding comes from Council Tax. With the changes to the funding system this is even more apparent with 65% of GCC's base budget being funded from Council Tax in 2026/27, increasing to 72% by 2028/29.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Draft Budget and MTFS
findings.headline: Council is losing its business rates pooling arrangement, resulting in a permanent loss of £1.1 million per year of previously reliable income.
findings.detail: GCC has participated in a business rates pooling arrangement since 2013/14 that provided additional income. With changes to the Business Rates Retention Scheme, the pooling gains have been eliminated: 'With the changes to the BRRS, levies have been amended and set at 10% for all districts and pools, meaning that there is no longer a gain from pooling. As a result, and following discussions with the districts no pooling application has been submitted.'
findings.matters: The loss of £1.1m per year from a scheme running over a decade is a structural change in available revenue. This represents a known income source permanently removed, independent of service demand or cost pressures.
findings.figures: £1.1 million per year average pooling gain lost; £3.9 million average pooling gain historically
findings.quote: This is an unfortunate change to the system, as gains from pooling have been on average £3.9 million, with GCC receiving an average gain of £1.1 million per year.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Draft Budget and MTFS
findings.headline: Provisional funding settlement delivers an adverse impact of £9.5 million in 2026/27, growing to £34.9 million by 2029/30, despite appearing as a small CSP increase.
findings.detail: While the provisional settlement shows a £345k increase to CSP for 2026/27, this masks a £9.5 million underlying adverse impact because specific grants have been rolled into CSP and reduced through new Relative Needs Formulas. The document states: 'the true impact of the provisional settlement for 2026/27 is an adverse impact of £9.5 million compared to the December figures, and this adverse impact grows over the life of the MTFS.' The total adverse impact grows to £34.9 million by 2029/30.
findings.matters: A lender must understand that announced funding increases mask real resource reductions. The gap between headline settlement figures and usable funding is material and grows significantly over the forecast period.
findings.figures: £345k CSP increase in 2026/27; adverse impact of £9.5 million in 2026/27; adverse impact of £34.9 million by 2029/30
findings.quote: the true impact of the provisional settlement for 2026/27 is an adverse impact of £9.5 million compared to the December figures, and this adverse impact grows over the life of the MTFS

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Draft Budget and MTFS
findings.headline: Budget gaps of £9.4 million and £9.6 million remain unresolved for 2028/29 and 2029/30 with no identified solutions.
findings.detail: The 2026/27 and 2027/28 budgets are balanced through reserve use and changes to assumptions, but the council has not identified how to close gaps in the final two years of its medium-term plan. The document states: 'There remain budget gaps in 2028/29 and 2029/30 of £9.4 million and £9.6 million respectively, which will need to be addressed through additional funding and further efficiencies.' No specific proposals are identified.
findings.matters: Unresolved budget gaps with no identified solutions indicate the council's financial plan is incomplete. This suggests either optimism about future government funding increases or expectation of further unplanned service reductions.
findings.figures: £9.4 million gap 2028/29; £9.6 million gap 2029/30
findings.quote: There remain budget gaps in 2028/29 and 2029/30 of £9.4 million and £9.6 million respectively, which will need to be addressed through additional funding and further efficiencies.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Draft Budget and MTFS
findings.headline: DSG High Needs Block deficit forecast to exceed £241.6 million by March 2028, with ongoing deficits expected in future years.
findings.detail: The High Needs Block is in structural deficit supported only by a Statutory Override allowing ring-fenced deficit balances. The forecast deficit as at 31 March 2026 is £124.1 million, with anticipated deficits of £54.4 million in 2026/27 and £63.1 million in 2027/28. The document explicitly states: 'Given the ongoing funding challenges with High Needs services, it is expected that deficits will continue in future years unless additional funding is allocated and reforms to SEND legislation are implemented.'
findings.matters: An unsustainable ringfenced deficit exceeding £241m indicates a service allocation problem that cannot be resolved within current funding structures. This is a fundamental structural issue affecting the council's financial stability and borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: £124.1 million deficit at 31 March 2026; £54.4 million deficit budget 2026/27; £63.1 million deficit budget 2027/28; cumulative deficit beyond £241.6 million by 31 March 2028
findings.quote: The forecast deficit balance as of 31 March 2026 is £124.1 million. Based on current information (without any resetting of the High Needs allocations) it is anticipated that a deficit budget of £54.4 million will be set in 2026/27 and £63.1 million in 2027/28. This will increase the cumulative deficit beyond £241.6 million by the expected end of Statutory Override on 31 March 2028.

findings.paper_title: For Cabinet - Corporate Asset Management Plan 2026-2029_v3 - Copy
findings.headline: Plan acknowledges risk that short-term property investment costs may not align with long-term savings benefits during Service Estate Plan implementation
findings.detail: The risks section explicitly identifies 'a risk there could be a mismatch between short-term investment and long-term cost savings' as detailed Service Estate Plans are developed. The council proposes to manage this through options appraisals, but timing uncertainty is acknowledged.
findings.matters: Signals that assumed savings benefits may not materialise on planned timescales; benefit realisation depends on sound options appraisal and effective project delivery
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: As detailed Service Estate Plans are developed, there is a risk there could be a mismatch between short-term investment and long-term cost savings. The risk will be managed through developing detailed options appraisals against which the Council will be able to make sound business decisions.

findings.paper_title: For Cabinet - Corporate Asset Management Plan 2026-2029_v3 - Copy
findings.headline: Council's MTFS savings delivery depends on successful property rationalisation from Local Government Reorganisation
findings.detail: The plan states it will support delivery of savings plans in the MTFS 'including Agile Phase 2, Local Government Reorganisation, capital receipts delivery.' This links the council's budgeted savings to successful completion of LGR property consolidation and office agile working initiatives, both of which carry execution risk.
findings.matters: Identified savings realization depends on successful LGR transition and property consolidation; either could slip or take longer than forecast, jeopardising MTFS delivery
findings.figures: £2 million previously invested in solar panels on maintained schools (mentioned as example of capital spend)
findings.quote: the plan will support the delivery of savings plans included within the Medium Term Financial Strategy including Agile Phase 2, Local Government Reorganisation, capital receipts delivery, maintenance of the estate and the reduction in carbon emissions.

findings.paper_title: For Cabinet - Corporate Asset Management Plan 2026-2029_v3 - Copy
findings.headline: Capital programme includes two new 200-place all-through special schools and three new care homes, already funded
findings.detail: The plan confirms capital commitments for special education provision (new schools in Gloucester and Cheltenham) and adult social care infrastructure (three new care homes) that are already included in the capital programme with funding secured. These represent significant ongoing investment in demand-led services.
findings.matters: Confirms extent of approved capital commitments in special education and social care, which are demand-exposed areas for councils
findings.figures: Two 200-place-all-through special schools in Gloucester (2027) and Cheltenham (2028); three new care homes
findings.quote: Service property requirements identified and already in the capital programme with funding include two new 200-place-all-through special schools in Gloucester (2027) and Cheltenham (2028), three new care homes and new and improved ways to deliver training for our fire service colleagues in appropriate locations.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - S151 Officer Review of the Budget - S25 Statement
findings.headline: Interest-rate volatility poses growing risk due to cashflow depletion from SEND deficits and increased borrowing dependency
findings.detail: The statement notes that interest-rate sensitivity is 'particularly relevant due to cashflow depletion linked to SEND deficits', which CIPFA has highlighted as a growing sector-wide risk. Stress testing models a 50bps rate increase as a 'severe but plausible' scenario.
findings.matters: As the council's free cashflow erodes from SEND deficits, increased borrowing becomes necessary; rising interest rates could significantly compress already tight budgets.
findings.figures: 50bps interest-rate increase modelled in stress testing
findings.quote: Interest-rate volatility, particularly relevant due to cashflow depletion linked to SEND deficits (a risk highlighted nationally)

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - S151 Officer Review of the Budget - S25 Statement
findings.headline: General Reserves described as 'adequate for 2026/27 but with very limited headroom' due to elevated volatility and demand pressures
findings.detail: The S151 Officer notes that with reduced contingencies, reserves must be preserved for genuine risk events and carry a greater burden managing volatility. Reserves remain above the minimum 5% policy but provide little buffer for emerging pressures.
findings.matters: Limited reserve headroom reduces the council's ability to absorb shocks in social care placement costs, SEND growth, or pay inflation without service cuts or further borrowing.
findings.figures: General Reserves remain above minimum 5% policy
findings.quote: Reserves are adequate for 2026/27 but with limited headroom. They must be protected due to heightened volatility from reduced contingencies, late funding notification, and demand-led pressures.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - S151 Officer Review of the Budget - S25 Statement
findings.headline: £1.4m of unearmarked reserves being used to balance 2026/27 budget, which S151 Officer says is 'not sustainable'
findings.detail: The council is drawing down unearmarked reserves to balance the budget. While the S151 Officer considers this 'acceptable for 2026/27', they explicitly state it is 'not sustainable', signalling this cannot continue in future years.
findings.matters: Ongoing reserve depletion indicates structural budget imbalance; the council cannot rely on one-off reserve use as a permanent solution.
findings.figures: £1.4 million
findings.quote: Planned use of £1.4m unearmarked reserves to balance the 2026/27 budget is acceptable but not sustainable.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - S151 Officer Review of the Budget - S25 Statement
findings.headline: Corporate contingencies for pay and inflation reduced due to late funding notification, materially increasing overspend risk
findings.detail: The council reduced contingency buffers following late government notification of a reduced funding settlement, requiring rapid budget adjustment. The S151 Officer states this increases 'the probability of in-year overspends' and 'less flexibility for emerging pressures.'
findings.matters: With smaller contingency buffers, adverse movements in pay awards, National Living Wage, or inflation can quickly exhaust reserves and force in-year spending controls.
findings.figures: No specific contingency figures disclosed
findings.quote: The Council reduced corporate contingencies for pay and inflation following late notification of a reduced funding settlement, requiring rapid adjustment. This increases the probability of: • In-year overspends • Less flexibility for emerging pressures

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - S151 Officer Review of the Budget - S25 Statement
findings.headline: If required to borrow for historic SEND deficits, council faces ongoing annual revenue cost of £10.8m
findings.detail: The council has modelled the scenario where government requires local authorities to borrow to finance historical DSG deficits. GCC estimates this would impose approximately £10.8m annual revenue costs reflecting the council's projected borrowing requirements, interest rate assumptions, and repayment profiles.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the downside scenario if government shifts liability to councils; £10.8m annual revenue cost would significantly constrain financial resilience.
findings.figures: £10.8 million annual revenue cost
findings.quote: If Government required local authorities to borrow to finance historical DSG deficits, GCC estimates that such an arrangement could impose ongoing annual revenue costs of approximately £10.8 million.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - S151 Officer Review of the Budget - S25 Statement
findings.headline: S151 Officer's Section 25 assurance is explicitly conditional on government funding SEND and maintaining the statutory override until March 2028
findings.detail: The S151 Officer states their professional assurance depends entirely on two conditions: the DSG override staying in place to March 2028, and government implementing a fully funded solution for both historic deficits and revenue costs of any repayment mechanism. If either fails, the officer says 'GCC's ability to remain financially sustainable in the medium term would be fundamentally undermined.'
findings.matters: A conditional S151 assurance signals the officer cannot give unconditional comfort on financial sustainability; it is contingent on external government action outside council control.
findings.figures: £14bn national sector SEND deficit forecast
findings.quote: My Section 25 assurance is explicitly conditional upon: 1. The DSG Statutory Override remaining in place until March 2028; and 2. Government implementing a fully funded national solution to both: o historic SEND deficits, and o revenue costs arising from whatever repayment mechanism is adopted. If these assumptions are not met, GCC's ability to remain financially sustainable in the medium term would be fundamentally undermined.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - S151 Officer Review of the Budget - S25 Statement
findings.headline: SEND/DSG deficit of £124.1m is the council's single most significant financial risk, currently deferred by statutory override expiring March 2028
findings.detail: Gloucestershire faces a cumulative SEND deficit of £124.1m from unfunded statutory duties under the Children and Families Act 2014. The deficit is excluded from General Funds by a national statutory override, but without a fully funded government solution by March 2028, most affected authorities risk having to issue a Section 114 notice.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether this council faces an immediate solvency crisis when the override ends, and whether government will actually fund a solution.
findings.figures: £124.1 million cumulative deficit; national sector modelling indicates £14bn cumulative SEND deficits by March 2028
findings.quote: By March 2026, Gloucestershire County Council (GCC) is forecast to hold approximately £124.1 million of cumulative DSG/SEND deficit arising from unfunded expenditure on statutory SEND duties. This represents the Council's single most significant financial risk.

findings.paper_title: Glouestershire County Council - ISA260 report 24-25 - final
findings.headline: Governance weakness: incomplete declarations of interest from councillors, creating unidentified conflict risk
findings.detail: Audit testing found three Councillors had not completed Declarations of Interest within the expected timeframe, and the Council could not obtain a declaration from a fourth Councillor. This creates a risk that conflicts of interest and related party transactions may go unidentified or undisclosed.
findings.matters: Incomplete conflict declarations could result in undisclosed related party transactions or financial decisions made with unidentified conflicts, affecting reporting integrity and exposing the council to reputational and compliance risk.
findings.figures: 3 late declarations, 1 unobtained declaration
findings.quote: During our testing of related party transactions, we identified that three Councillors had not completed Declarations of Interest within the expected timeframe and there was one Councillor for which the Council was unable to obtain a declaration.

findings.paper_title: Glouestershire County Council - ISA260 report 24-25 - final
findings.headline: Journal control deficiencies remain unresolved pending delayed SAP system implementation until 2026
findings.detail: Prior year audit findings identified control deficiencies in journal processing (missing descriptions, approvals outside the finance system, segregation of duties issues). These were expected to be resolved by cloud-based SAP implementation but that has been delayed until 2026. The auditors have explicitly not placed reliance on journal controls and do not expect to resolve this until the system change.
findings.matters: Unresolved journal control weaknesses increase the risk of unauthorized, unsupported, or erroneous financial transactions being processed without adequate review and approval, particularly material given the Council's transaction volumes.
findings.figures: System implementation delayed to 2026
findings.quote: There were control deficiencies noted in the prior year that are expected to be addressed by the new Cloud-based SAP system. As the implementation of the new SAP system has been delayed, we expect these deficiencies to continue to exist and have planned our audit work accordingly.

findings.paper_title: Glouestershire County Council - ISA260 report 24-25 - final
findings.headline: Auditors have identified significant weaknesses in the Council's financial sustainability arrangements
findings.detail: The audit has identified one significant risk in the Financial Sustainability domain for Value for Money (VFM), resulting in a conclusion that significant weaknesses exist in the Council's arrangements to secure economy, efficiency and effectiveness in use of resources. The specific findings and management recommendations are detailed in the separate Auditor's Annual Report provided to the Committee, but the core conclusion is that financial sustainability weaknesses have been identified.
findings.matters: A lender assessing creditworthiness needs confidence that the council has effective arrangements for managing resources efficiently and sustainably; significant weaknesses in this area directly indicate risks to long-term financial position.
findings.figures: One significant risk identified in financial sustainability domain
findings.quote: We have identified one risk of a significant weakness in the Council's arrangements to secure value for money. Within our Auditor's Annual Report we have set out our response to that risk and have set out recommendations in relation to the significant weakness identified.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Net annual interest cost of £3.3m (£11.5m debt service vs £8.2m investment income) forecast to deteriorate as rates fall and investment base shrinks
findings.detail: 2026/27: debt service £11.5m on £251m average portfolio at 4.5% average rate; investment income £8.2m at assumed 3.6% return on declining balances. Council forecasts investment income will fall further due to 'predicted falling interest rates and lower investment balances.' Each 1% fall in rates reduces investment income by approximately £1-1.2m on reducing asset base.
findings.matters: Deteriorating structural position. As rates fall and capital spending continues, council's net interest cost burden grows. Suggests medium-term need for either external funding sources or capital programme restraint to maintain budget balance.
findings.figures: £8.2 million investment income 2026/27, £11.5 million debt interest 2026/27, 4.5% average debt rate, 3.6% assumed investment rate
findings.quote: The expected investment income in 2026/27 is forecast to be £8.2 million. Future investment income is forecast to be lower due to predicted falling interest rates and lower investment balances as a result of the internally borrowed position.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: £2.198m portfolio loss locked in by fossil fuel disinvestment policy; forces council to hold depressed assets until value recovery
findings.detail: Council holds three funds (Aegon, Ninety One, Schroders) containing fossil fuel investments. 2019 council motion prohibits new fossil fuel investments. Cannot exit without crystallizing £2.198m loss. Council must hold these positions below par value awaiting capital recovery, constraining portfolio optimization and diversification strategy.
findings.matters: Policy-driven constraint on treasury flexibility. If market stress occurs or council urgently needs cash, unable to rebalance portfolio without realizing loss. Creates asymmetric downside in market shock scenarios.
findings.figures: £2.198 million loss on three fossil fuel-containing funds, improvement of £0.5 million from March 2025
findings.quote: Three of the funds currently held contain fossil fuel investment (Aegon, Ninety One and Schroders), and the loss currently reported on those funds is £2.198 million, an improvement of over £0.5 million on values at the end of March 2025.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: £4.0m unrealized loss on strategic investment funds will hit budget from March 2029 when statutory accounting override expires
findings.detail: Council currently holds strategic pooled funds with £4.0m cumulative losses (£2.25m excluding social housing REIT). These losses are not recognized in budget due to statutory override of mark-to-market accounting. Override ends March 2029, at which point any remaining losses must be budgeted for. Document notes social housing REIT (Fundamentum) particularly affected by 'distressed housing associations' and 'lack of clear government policy.'
findings.matters: Known future budget pressure with material quantum. Timing depends on fund recovery, but at least £2.25m may hit revenue budget from 2029/30. Creates contingent liability in forward budget planning.
findings.figures: £4.0 million total capital loss, £2.25 million excluding Fundamentum REIT, £4.2 million loss prior year
findings.quote: This override is coming to an end in March 2029, at which point any gains and losses will need to be taken into account when the Budget is set.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Three LOBO loans (£22.05m) held at 6-monthly lender call option; council flagged for repayment in 2026/27 if called
findings.detail: Council holds 3 Lender Option Borrower Option loans with Dexia Bank totaling £22.05m at 4.35% average rate. LOBOs carry lender call options every 6 months. Document states council views these loans as having 'inflexible structure and long life' and intends to repay them if called during 2026/27. Current external debt portfolio averages 4.57%, indicating rates have moved against this position.
findings.matters: Refinancing risk if lender exercises call. If called and rates remain elevated above 4.35%, council faces higher refinancing cost. Material for forward interest rate exposure.
findings.figures: £22.05 million LOBO exposure, 4.35% average LOBO rate, 4.57% average all external borrowing rate
findings.quote: GCC has 3 Lender Option Borrower Option (LOBO's) with Dexia Bank on a 6 monthly call. If these were called GCC will take the opportunity to repay these loans during 2026/27 due to their inflexible structure and long life.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Treasury investment balances falling rapidly; council itself flags potential liquidity stress if external borrowing not accessed
findings.detail: Investment holdings ranged between £173.6m and £291.5m during 2025/26, with minimum balances £47.6m lower than prior year. Forecast to fall to £138m by March 2026 as balances are used to fund capital schemes. Council explicitly states this trajectory creates risk: 'short-term liquidity issues may arise if debt is not externalised.'
findings.matters: Declining liquidity buffer narrows options. If council urgently needs cash and cannot access debt markets, would be forced to defer spending or cut reserves further. Council notes they manage year-end borrowing to avoid taking debt when 'rates can be artificially high.'
findings.figures: £291.5 million (high), £173.6 million at 31/12/25, £138 million forecast March 2026
findings.quote: Investment balances are falling as borrowing continues to be held internally and short-term liquidity issues may arise if debt is not externalised.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Capital financing requirement rising to £495m with 20-year external borrowing horizon ahead
findings.detail: CFR was £484.5m at March 2025 and forecast to rise to £495m by March 2026. Council is deliberately holding debt internally (using investment balances to offset borrowing need) rather than externalizing to PWLB. Document's liability benchmark chart indicates council faces 20-year structural borrowing need due to approved capital programme.
findings.matters: Forward-looking indicator of refinancing cliff. As investment balances become exhausted, council will need to externalize large debt amounts, creating refinancing risk exposure at whatever rates prevail.
findings.figures: £484.5 million CFR at March 2025, £495.2 million forecast March 2026, £228.4 million external borrowing, £136.6 million lease liability
findings.quote: The benchmark indicates a rising CFR over the current MTFS period due to the approved capital programme. This indicates that GCC will need to manage debt in the short term with the chart indicating a 20-year borrowing need.

findings.paper_title: Gloucestershire County Council - Auditors Annual Report 24-25 (final)
findings.headline: Adult Social Care assessed by CQC as 'Requires Improvement' in January 2025
findings.detail: The Care Quality Commission assessed the council's Adult Social Care in January 2025 and rated it as 'Requires Improvement', aligning with the council's own self-assessment. The rating was discussed at the Adult Social Care and Communities Scrutiny Committee in March 2025. Adult Social Care is typically one of the largest budget areas for a county council.
findings.matters: A 'Requires Improvement' rating in Adult Social Care indicates service quality and governance challenges in what is typically a council's largest controllable budget. Combined with £4.7m of unachieved savings in this same service, it suggests the service is under stress and likely to face further cost pressures.
findings.figures: Not specified in the report
findings.quote: In January 2025, CQC published a local authority assessment which was Requires Improvement.

findings.paper_title: Gloucestershire County Council - Auditors Annual Report 24-25 (final)
findings.headline: Finance system has known control weaknesses over journal entries, pending replacement with new SAP system
findings.detail: The auditor identified known weaknesses in the current finance system relating to journal controls, including journals with missing descriptions and journals approved outside the finance system. These are expected to be addressed when a new cloud-based SAP system is implemented. However, the system replacement has been delayed; it was included in the Annual Governance Statement action plan for both 2023/24 and 2024/25, indicating delays spanning multiple years.
findings.matters: Journal entry controls are fundamental to financial control. Weaknesses in this area create risk of undetected errors or misstatements. The persistence of these weaknesses across multiple years, combined with delays to the replacement system, raises questions about the council's financial control environment and management of its transformation risk.
findings.figures: Not specified in the report
findings.quote: There are known weaknesses in current finance system in relation to journal controls, such as journals with missing descriptions and journals approved outside of the finance system. These weaknesses are expected to be addressed when the new cloud-based SAP system is implemented.

findings.paper_title: Gloucestershire County Council - Auditors Annual Report 24-25 (final)
findings.headline: £6m of required savings not delivered in 2024/25, with Adult Social Care accounting for £4.7m of the shortfall
findings.detail: The council delivered £26.4 million of savings against a target of £32.5 million, leaving a £6 million shortfall. Of this, £4.7 million was due to unachieved savings in Adult Social Care, with the council noting that this service is "developing plans for their permanent delivery". This 18% shortfall against a key service suggests the council's savings assumptions may not be realistic, particularly given Adult Social Care's demand-led nature and scale.
findings.matters: When a council fails to deliver significant savings commitments, it signals weak financial planning or inability to execute service changes. A lender needs confidence that budgeted savings are achievable, especially in Adult Social Care, typically the largest controllable budget and a key source of financial risk across local government.
findings.figures: £26.4 million savings delivered against £32.5 million target; £4.7 million unachieved in Adults Services
findings.quote: During the year, the Council delivered £26.4 million of savings against a savings target of £32.5 million. Of the £6 million unachieved 2024/25 savings, £4.7 million related to Adults Services and £1.9 million is expected to be delivered in 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: Gloucestershire County Council - Auditors Annual Report 24-25 (final)
findings.headline: DSG deficit identified as significant weakness, increased by £32.8m in one year with forecast to exceed £110m by March 2026
findings.detail: The auditor identified the growing Dedicated Schools Grant deficit as a significant weakness in financial sustainability arrangements. The deficit increased by £32.8 million in 2024/25 to £78.5 million, compared to a General Fund balance of £36.8 million. Five-year modelling predicts the deficit could exceed £110 million by 31 March 2026. The council's recovery plan is still in development with the Department for Education and Schools Forum, but has not been formalized. If the current statutory override protecting General Fund balances is removed (extended to March 2028), the council would be required to cover the deficit from its General Fund.
findings.matters: A lender must understand whether the council has a credible, formal plan to address a £78.5m deficit growing at £32.8m per year. The lack of formalization combined with the scale and pace of the forecast deficit raises serious questions about medium-term financial sustainability.
findings.figures: DSG deficit £78.5 million (increased by £32.8 million in 2024/25); General Fund balance £36.8 million; 5-year forecast predicts deficit could exceed £110 million by 31 March 2026
findings.quote: We are aware that a plan for the DSG deficit is in development with the DfE and with the Schools Forum, but insufficient progress has been made to formalise the plan and set out a pathway to recovery.

findings.paper_title: Gloucestershire County Council - ISA260 report 24-25
findings.headline: Capital programme of £198.8m assessed for expenditure recognition risk
findings.detail: Given the size of the Council's capital programme (£198.8m), auditors identified an other audit risk regarding whether revenue expenditure is being inaccurately recognised as capital expenditure that can be funded from capital sources. Testing found no issues, but this remains a control area requiring ongoing attention.
findings.matters: Misclassification between revenue and capital expenditure can distort the council's spending profile, impact reserves, and affect financial planning and borrowing requirements.
findings.figures: Council capital programme: £198.8m
findings.quote: Given the size of the Council's capital programme (£198.8m), we have identified an Other Audit Risk regarding revenue expenditure being inaccurately recognised as expenditure that can be funded from capital sources.

findings.paper_title: Gloucestershire County Council - ISA260 report 24-25
findings.headline: Energy from Waste facility valued at £186m is subject to specialist valuation challenge
findings.detail: The Energy from Waste facility, valued at £186m, represents a significant proportion of the £457m land and buildings revalued in the year (out of £980m total). This specialised operational asset involves significant judgement on obsolescence assumptions and is valued by two independent external valuers (Avison Young and Hilco). Auditors engaged a property valuation specialist to challenge the methodology.
findings.matters: Large specialised assets with significant valuation judgement and high potential for material misstatement are important to lenders assessing the council's asset base and borrowing capacity, particularly for any facility that may be income-generating.
findings.figures: Energy from Waste facility valued at £186m (of £457m revalued in year, from £980m total Land & Building assets)
findings.quote: The valuation involves significant judgement and estimation on behalf of the Council's valuers. We consider this to apply to specialised assets, specifically the obsolescence assumptions for the Energy from Waste specialised operational asset... the Energy from Waste facility is valued at £186m

findings.paper_title: Gloucestershire County Council - ISA260 report 24-25
findings.headline: Significant pension liability of £1.43bn with substantial year-on-year movement
findings.detail: The present value of defined benefit obligation (LGPS pension liability) stands at £1,428.1m, down £207.3m from prior year. This is a significant accounting estimate involving inherently subjective actuarial assumptions. The auditors assessed overall assumptions as balanced within reasonable range, but future mortality assumption was cautious.
findings.matters: Large pension liabilities are a material component of council liabilities and impact long-term financial sustainability. Significant year-on-year movements and the subjective nature of actuarial assumptions mean changes in assumptions could materially impact the council's balance sheet.
findings.figures: Present value of defined benefit obligation: £1,428.1m (down £207.3m from prior year); Fair value of LGPS assets: £1,681.1m (up £76.2m)
findings.quote: The selection of these assumptions is inherently subjective and small changes in the assumptions and estimates used to value the Council's pension liability could have a significant effect on the financial position of the Council.

findings.paper_title: Gloucestershire County Council - ISA260 report 24-25
findings.headline: Journal control deficiencies from prior year remain unresolved pending delayed SAP system implementation
findings.detail: Control weaknesses noted in the prior year regarding journals with missing descriptions, journals approved outside the finance system, and deficiencies in segregation of duties are expected to be addressed by a new cloud-based SAP system. However, the implementation has been delayed until 2026, meaning these deficiencies continue to exist and are still relevant to 2024/25.
findings.matters: Unresolved control deficiencies around journal approval increase fraud risk and the potential for management override of controls, which is a significant audit risk for any organisation handling large financial transactions.
findings.figures: SAP system implementation delayed to 2026; prior year journal control weaknesses remain unaddressed in 2024/25
findings.quote: There were control deficiencies noted in the prior year that are expected to be addressed by the new Cloud-based SAP system. As the implementation of the new SAP system has been delayed, we expect these deficiencies to continue to exist

findings.paper_title: Gloucestershire County Council - ISA260 report 24-25
findings.headline: Audit procedures incomplete at report date with significant matters still in progress
findings.detail: At the time of writing, the audit was not fully complete. Outstanding items include testing of high-risk journals, final sample testing, disclosure review, Annual Governance Statement consistency check, and awaiting CIPFA guidance on IFRS 9 impact. Final conclusions will be discussed before audit report signature.
findings.matters: An incomplete audit with outstanding journal testing and control assessments means audit conclusions and potential findings could still change before final sign-off, particularly relevant given prior-year journal control deficiencies.
findings.figures: Multiple outstanding audit procedures including high-risk journal testing, final sample testing, disclosure review, Annual Governance Statement check, and CIPFA IFRS 9 guidance awaited
findings.quote: At the time of drafting this report, our audit is not yet fully complete and matters communicated in this Report may change pending signature of our audit report.

findings.paper_title: Mid Year Treasury Report Sept AGC 2025
findings.headline: Council sustaining £35m in short-term loans at volatile rates, indicating tight cash buffer
findings.detail: As of 31st August 2025, four short-term loans totalling £35m remain outstanding to manage cashflow gaps between capital expenditure and available cash. Interest rates on these loans range from 4.45% to 5.8% depending on market conditions. The council's treasury advisors recommend keeping borrowing short-term given current long-term rates above 6%, but this strategy exposes the council to rate and refinancing risk.
findings.matters: Reliance on £35m of short-term borrowing indicates limited cash buffer; any disruption to short-term money markets or a sharp rates rise could create acute liquidity pressure
findings.figures: £35m in outstanding short-term loans as at 31/08/2025, rates 4.45%-5.8% depending on term, PWLB long-term rates currently over 6%
findings.quote: As at 31st August 2025, 4 short term loans remain outstanding totalling £35 million, the 4 loans outstanding are shown shaded below.

findings.paper_title: Mid Year Treasury Report Sept AGC 2025
findings.headline: Strategic fund portfolio carries £2.25m unrealised losses due to become revenue-exposed from March 2029
findings.detail: The council holds £85m in strategic funds (equities, property, multi-asset) with current unrealised losses of £2.25m. A statutory override currently shields the revenue account from capital value fluctuations, but this expires March 2029. After that date, capital losses must be funded from revenue. The council has established a smoothing reserve but its adequacy is not detailed.
findings.matters: This creates a structural revenue budget pressure from 2029 onwards; capital market volatility will directly impact the council's ability to fund services and could constrain borrowing headroom
findings.figures: Strategic funds £90.0m total invested, current unrealised loss £2.25m, override extends to March 2029, £85m of investments subject to override impact
findings.quote: Ending of the override will put pressures on budgets, as fluctuations in capital value, particularly reduced values, will need to be funded. To this effect a smoothing reserve has been established with a provision being built into the GF Reserve that was approved by Council in February 2024.

findings.paper_title: Mid Year Treasury Report Sept AGC 2025
findings.headline: Internal cash resources forecast exhausted by 2027/28, forcing external borrowing at unknown future rates
findings.detail: The council's internal borrowing position of £119.6m will be consumed by 2027/28 based on current capital spend profiles. External borrowing will then be required to fund capital schemes and maintain liquidity. This represents a material funding strategy change and will lock the council into whatever interest rates prevail at that time, currently projected as high.
findings.matters: A lender needs visibility on when the council's self-funding capacity runs out and external market access becomes essential; the timing matters for both the council and creditors evaluating refinancing risk
findings.figures: Internal borrowing £119.6m as at 31/03/2025, CFR forecast to increase from £484.5m to £667.4m by 2029, current long-term rates over 6%
findings.quote: Based on these forecasts GCC is expected to have used all cash resources by 2027/28 and externalisation of borrowing would be needed from this point.

findings.paper_title: Mid Year Treasury Report Sept AGC 2025
findings.headline: LOBO loans carry 30% call risk in November 2025 requiring potential costlier refinancing
findings.detail: The council holds LOBO loans callable every six months, with the next call date in November 2025. Market conditions have reduced the probability to 30%, but if called, the council would repay these loans and replace the shortfall with short-term borrowing at higher rates than the current long-term fixed rates over 6%.
findings.matters: A called LOBO loan would force unplanned refinancing at unfavorable rates in an already tight liquidity position; the council notes it will resort to short-term loans if called, locking in higher ongoing costs
findings.figures: Next call date November 2025, 30% probability of call, current short-term rates 4.45%-5.8%, long-term rates over 6%
findings.quote: The LOBO loans held are at risk of being called every six months. The next call date is November 2025; however, the expectation of call has reduced to 30% following changes in market rates.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement 2024-25 v4 Final signed
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation creating resource and workforce stability risks requiring monitoring
findings.detail: English Devolution White Paper and statutory invitation for local government reorganisation has fundamentally changed the council's operating environment. Significant resource has been diverted to respond to government deadlines (initial 21 March, final 28 November 2025). Governance risks identified include workforce stability and retention due to uncertainty, high levels of concurrent transformation activity straining capacity, and potential partner relationship tensions.
findings.matters: Organisational uncertainty and competing transformation priorities create risk of distraction from financial management priorities and core service delivery; programme likely to continue until April 2028, prolonging uncertainty.
findings.figures: Programme timeline to April 2028; final submission deadline 28 November 2025
findings.quote: Significant resource has already been diverted to respond to the government's initial deadline of 21st March with further planning in place to progress towards final submissions on 28th November 2025.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement 2024-25 v4 Final signed
findings.headline: Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) system implementation missed 31 March 2025 go-live; payroll data migration challenges
findings.detail: The One SAP programme reset in 2023/24 established revised governance and timeline. However, despite good progress during 2024/25, the planned 31 March go-live date could not be met due to challenges with payroll data migration. The programme is being remapped and a revised go-live date will be agreed with implementation partner HCL and SAP, currently anticipated for early 2026.
findings.matters: ERP delay extends period of legacy system operational risk and defers benefits realisation; impacts on financial reporting controls and procurement visibility until new system live.
findings.figures: Missed 31 March 2025 go-live; revised date anticipated early 2026
findings.quote: Whilst good progress has been made over the course of 2024/25 to implement the cloud based SAP system, it has not been possible to meet the planned 31st March go-live date due to challenges with the payroll data migration.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement 2024-25 v4 Final signed
findings.headline: Procurement and contract management oversight weaknesses identified, particularly within directorates
findings.detail: Council has identified weaknesses in arrangements for overseeing procurement and contract management, particularly where activity is undertaken within directorates rather than centrally. External audit has flagged this issue. Actions undertaken include refreshing the contract management framework, improved use of procurement pipeline, and reporting of direct awards to Audit & Governance Committee. Introduction of Procurement Act 2023 in February 2025 brings new compliance requirements and increased visibility.
findings.matters: Control weaknesses in procurement increase risk of contract overspend, poor value for money, and compliance failure; new system implementation will expose any embedded compliance issues.
findings.figures: Procurement Act 2023 commenced February 2025; new ERP system implementation underway
findings.quote: The Council has identified weaknesses in its arrangements for overseeing procurement and contract management, particularly where that activity is undertaken within Directorates, rather than centrally by the Strategic Procurement Team.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement 2024-25 v4 Final signed
findings.headline: Adult Social Care rated 'requires improvement' by CQC; council committing additional £5.6m over two years to transformation
findings.detail: CQC full assessment in September 2024 rated Adult Social Care 'requires improvement', matching the council's own self-assessment. Inspectors found mixed experiences for service users with inconsistencies across the county. The council is investing an additional £5.6m on transformation over the next two years on top of £224.264m already approved in the 2025/26 budget, reflecting both the scale of service challenges and council commitment to improvement.
findings.matters: Significant unplanned additional investment signals pressure on service delivery and financial commitments beyond baseline budget; outcomes remain uncertain pending progress visit.
findings.figures: £5.6m additional investment over two years; £224.264m committed to adult social care in 2025/26 budget approved February 2025
findings.quote: The council is investing an additional £5.6m in its adults transformation plans over the next two years. This is in addition to the £224.264m already committed to adult social care in the 2025/26 budget which was approved by full council in February 2025.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement 2024-25 v4 Final signed
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit creating structural pressure on reserves and financial sustainability
findings.detail: The council operates with a growing DSG deficit driven by rising high needs demand and SEND Code of Practice changes. External auditors have flagged inadequate arrangements to prevent deficit growth. A statutory override currently defers the problem, but its removal would force the full deficit onto General Fund balances. The council has modelled additional mitigation options but found none provide a pathway to a balanced in-year budget without materially impacting education provision.
findings.matters: Unresolved structural deficit threatens long-term financial stability and constrains the cash available for investment and day-to-day operations, creating dependency on national solution that remains uncertain.
findings.figures: Statutory override currently deferred; impact modelled across range of scenarios; reliance on General Fund balances if override removed
findings.quote: If the current statutory override was to be removed the deficit would need to be met through the use of General Fund balances, putting pressure on budgets and financial sustainability.

findings.paper_title: For Cabinet - SEND and AP Change Programme Lead LA MOU 2025-2026 - unsigned
findings.headline: Council is responsible for ensuring Partner Local Authorities' compliance with programme requirements and reporting standards
findings.detail: As Lead LA, Gloucestershire must understand all funding decisions across the partnership and ensure all Partner LAs meet programme requirements. If Partner LAs do not comply or perform adequately, they may be removed from the programme, affecting the partnership's delivery and funding.
findings.matters: The council's continued access to full funding depends partly on other authorities' compliance with reporting and programme requirements, creating external dependency and potential risk if Partner LAs underperform or miss deadlines.
findings.figures: Two to four Partner Local Authorities per partnership
findings.quote: Lead LAs must understand all funding decisions across the CPP, including those by Partner LAs. They must track committed and forecasted spend against actual spend.

findings.paper_title: For Cabinet - SEND and AP Change Programme Lead LA MOU 2025-2026 - unsigned
findings.headline: All Change Programme grant must be spent or committed by 31 March 2026; unspent funds are clawed back
findings.detail: The MOU requires all funding to be spent by March 2026 with no carry-forward. Final payments depend on actual and committed spend. Any underspend must be reported by 31 December 2025. The Department for Education will adjust future payments based on actual spend.
findings.matters: The council must commit and spend between £2.1 million and £3.5 million depending on partnership size within a single financial year, creating a tight spending requirement and cash commitment risk.
findings.figures: £2,071,167.16 (2-area partnership) to £3,476,739.67 (4-area partnership); deadline 31 March 2026
findings.quote: All funding must be spent by March 2026. The final payment will be based solely on actual and committed spend.

findings.paper_title: For Cabinet - SEND and AP Change Programme Lead LA MOU 2025-2026 - unsigned
findings.headline: Missing three consecutive monthly reports triggers funding suspension for this grant stream
findings.detail: The Lead LA must submit accurate monthly progress and financial reports to the Department for Education. The MOU explicitly states that if reports are missed for three consecutive months or are inaccurate, this will be escalated and may result in reduced or delayed funding. This applies to both operational progress reports and financial reports.
findings.matters: A finance director must ensure adequate reporting capacity and discipline to avoid suspension of multi-million pound grant funding supporting SEND and AP services.
findings.figures: three consecutive months
findings.quote: If reports are missed for three consecutive months or are inaccurate, this will be escalated to the Change Programme's Senior Leadership and to Directors of Children's Services or Directors of Education. This may lead to reduced or delayed funding.
